title: Mycorrhizal fungi and forest soil carbon
bodyMd:
For decades, models of forest carbon storage treated soil largely as a passive reservoir: carbon entered it when leaves and roots decayed, and left it when microbes respired. Recent work on mycorrhizal fungi complicates that picture. These fungi, which trade mineral nutrients to trees in exchange for sugars, channel a substantial fraction of a tree's photosynthetic output directly into the soil, bypassing litterfall entirely. Where such fungi dominate, soils can accumulate carbon even as the annual input of dead leaves and twigs declines.

The implications are not uniformly encouraging. Because the fungi are supplied by living trees, the flow is interrupted the moment a stand is cut, and the fungal networks themselves decay quickly once their hosts are gone. A forest managed on a short harvest rotation may therefore hold far less soil carbon than the size of its standing trees would suggest, and any inventory that estimates soil carbon from litter production alone will misstate how much is lost at harvest. Ackerly has argued that the discrepancy is large enough to change which management regimes look best; others reply that the effect, though real, has been extrapolated from an unrepresentative handful of temperate sites.

The first paragraph explains that older models treated soil as a passive store filled by decaying leaves and roots, and that mycorrhizal fungi complicate this by sending sugars from living trees straight into the soil without passing through leaf litter. The second paragraph explains that this carbon flow stops when trees are cut, so short-rotation forests may store less soil carbon than expected and litter-based inventories misstate harvest losses. A researcher named Ackerly considers the discrepancy large enough to change how management regimes rank; other researchers reply that the finding rests on too few temperate sites.
